papers.title: SFUMATO: Bayesian probabilistic clustering for uncertainty-aware spatial transcriptomics analysis and mapping
papers.summary: SFUMATO is a new computational method that uses Bayesian probabilistic modeling to cluster spatial transcriptomics data while explicitly capturing uncertainty in the clustering assignments. Unlike standard clustering approaches that give a single hard label per spatial location, SFUMATO provides probability distributions over cluster identities, reflecting ambiguity at boundaries or in mixed-cell-type regions. This uncertainty-aware approach is intended to improve the reliability and interpretability of spatial maps derived from tissue transcriptomic data.
papers.why: Robust, uncertainty-quantified clustering of spatial transcriptomics data could improve identification of interneuron subtypes and perineuronal net-associated niches in brain tissue, which is central to the spatial transcriptomics component of this PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing spatial maps of tissue sections colored by cluster assignment alongside corresponding uncertainty/probability maps, ideally in brain tissue.

papers.title: NexuST: A Hierarchical Foundation Model for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.summary: NexuST is a new foundation model designed to analyze spatial transcriptomics data using a hierarchical deep learning architecture. It likely aims to capture multi-scale patterns in tissue, from individual cells to broader spatial regions, improving tasks like cell-type annotation and spatial pattern discovery. As a foundation model, it is probably pretrained on large datasets and can be fine-tuned for specific downstream applications.
papers.why: This tool could be directly applied to the PhD project's spatial transcriptomics analysis of neurons and perineuronal nets, potentially improving classification of interneuron subtypes and spatial gene expression patterns relevant to mitophagy research.

papers.title: OpenFISH enables same-section spatial transcriptomics and MALDI-MSI integration.
papers.summary: OpenFISH is a new method that allows researchers to perform spatial transcriptomics (mapping gene expression locations) and MALDI mass spectrometry imaging (mapping molecule/metabolite distributions) on the very same tissue section. This avoids the need to use adjacent sections or separate samples, which can introduce alignment errors between the two data types. By combining both techniques directly on one slide, researchers can more precisely correlate gene expression patterns with metabolic or molecular signatures in the same cells and tissue regions.
papers.why: This technique directly supports integrating spatial transcriptomics and spatial metabolomics on the same tissue section, which is central to studying mitophagy, autophagy, interneurons, and perineuronal nets with multimodal spatial resolution.

papers.title: Neuropeptide Y and brain ageing: an updated scoping review on the role of autophagy
papers.summary: This paper is a scoping review examining how Neuropeptide Y (NPY) relates to brain ageing through its effects on autophagy. It likely synthesizes existing literature on NPY's regulatory role in cellular clearance mechanisms and how this changes with age. The review aims to update current understanding of this neuropeptide-autophagy relationship as it pertains to brain health and ageing processes.
papers.why: Understanding NPY's regulation of autophagy in ageing neurons could reveal upstream signaling pathways relevant to mitophagy dysregulation, particularly in interneuron populations studied in this project.

papers.title: UBE2D3-mediated ubiquitination of ULK1 drives pathological mitophagy and cuproptosis in myocardial infarction
papers.summary: This paper investigates how an enzyme called UBE2D3 adds ubiquitin tags to another protein, ULK1, a key initiator of autophagy/mitophagy. This ubiquitination process appears to trigger excessive, damaging mitophagy (clearance of mitochondria) alongside cuproptosis, a form of cell death linked to copper accumulation. The study focuses on heart tissue damage during myocardial infarction, showing this pathway contributes to cardiac injury.
papers.why: While this is a cardiac study, it offers mechanistic insight into ULK1 ubiquitination as a driver of pathological mitophagy, a regulatory concept that may be relevant to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neurons.

papers.title: Decoding Mitophagy in Breast Cancer: Biological Mechanisms, Dual Roles, and Clinical Implications.
papers.summary: This paper reviews mitophagy, the process by which cells selectively degrade damaged mitochondria, in the context of breast cancer. It discusses the biological mechanisms controlling mitophagy and how it can either suppress or promote tumor growth depending on context. The authors also cover potential clinical applications, such as using mitophagy pathways as biomarkers or therapeutic targets in breast cancer treatment.
papers.why: Although focused on breast cancer rather than neurons, this review may offer useful background on core mitophagy mechanisms and regulatory pathways that could inform interpretation of mitophagy processes in neuronal and brain contexts.

papers.title: AFF4 Loss Compromises Osteogenesis of Orofacial Mesenchymal Stem Cells During Alveolar Bone Repair via AMPK-Mediated Mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study examines how loss of the protein AFF4 affects the ability of orofacial mesenchymal stem cells to form bone during alveolar bone repair. The researchers found that AFF4 deficiency impairs osteogenesis (bone-forming capacity) through excessive mitophagy, the process by which damaged mitochondria are cleared from cells, regulated by the AMPK signaling pathway. This suggests AFF4 normally helps balance mitochondrial quality control to support proper bone regeneration in the jaw.
papers.why: While focused on bone repair rather than neurons, this paper offers a useful mechanistic parallel for AMPK-mediated mitophagy regulation that could inform how similar pathways are studied in neuronal mitochondrial quality control.
